<reason>CON (A) kept the debate on the motion as written and won the decisive clashes through adaptation. PRO's defenses required serial redefinitions—"activation is the opt-in," signup consent for fraud models, security-function exemptions—that A exposed as contradicting B's own stated standards (B1.3's multi-party rule, B2.6's consent-theater dismissal). B's smartest move, the consent-or-de-identify fork, was turned against it: A showed the fallback is A's own remedy, leaving the gate either unobtainable (stranger correspondents) or counterfeit (checkboxes). B retained a live prevention-before-irreversible-harm frame and extracted an honest unlearning concession, but its closing misdescribed the record twice (claiming "silence" on a question A answered in A4.4, and recasting A's de-identify-at-ingestion remedy as purely after-the-fact output policing) and was clipped for exceeding the cap. A's closing crystallized a clean decision rule; B's rested on a mischaracterization A had no turn left to correct.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A4): answered the unlearning pressure with an epistemically honest "None—and I won't fake one," pivoted to the layered remedy, then quoted B4.1's "the motion does cover it—and should" as an on-the-record overbreadth confession and converted B's de-identification fallback into proof the consent gate adds nothing—collapsing PRO's late route to victory in a single turn.</best_rebuttal>
